messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo presents as a well-groomed 24-year-old financial analyst, though his posture is tense and his eye contact fleeting. He secured a competitive position at a downtown firm shortly after his honorable discharge six months ago, a transition that, on paper, appears seamless. Internally, however, Mateo is struggling to stay afloat in the wake of his deployment in Afghanistan. The event that haunts him occurred during a routine patrol through a sprawling, sun-baked market square. He remembers the heat, the smell of spices and dust, and the unnerving quiet that fell just before the blast. An IED, concealed in a vendor’s cart, detonated ten feet from his position. The memory is not a coherent narrative but a series of disjointed, high-definition snapshots: the brilliant flash, the deafening roar that felt like a physical blow, the image of his friend, Corporal Evans, thrown against a wall. He can recall the exact colour of the dust that filled the air, but he cannot place these fragments in the right order, leaving him with a sense of perpetual, unresolved chaos.

These sudden pieces of the past ambush him without warning. Walking through the glass-walled lobby of his office building, a car backfiring on the street below can trigger a vivid flash of the explosion, so real he can almost feel the grit in his teeth. These intrusive memories serve as constant, brutal evidence for a belief he now holds as absolute: that he acted in ways that go against who he is. He is tormented by the thought that a better soldier, a better man, would have spotted the threat or reacted faster to save Evans. The memory, in its fragmented horror, feels like a verdict on his character, reinforcing his conviction that he is permanently an outsider, a man irrevocably separated from the civilians who surround him at his job. This certainty that he is fundamentally different and damaged makes him recoil from connection.

His deeply held negative appraisals of himself have become the architects of his daily life. The belief that he is a failure and has no future has hollowed out his motivation, but it is the conviction that he violated his core values that drives his most rigid behaviours. Because he sees himself as tainted by his actions—or inaction—during the ambush, he cannot bear to speak of the event. When well-meaning colleagues ask about his service, he offers vague, clipped responses, quickly changing the subject. This avoidance is a desperate attempt to keep his perceived shame contained. This pervasive sense of guilt and self-blame also seems to curate his memory; the moments that surface most often are those that highlight his perceived helplessness, while any memory of his own competence or the bravery of his unit remains inaccessible, buried under the weight of his negative self-assessment.

The interplay between memory and action has constricted his world to a tight, predictable loop. The sudden, vivid recollections of the attack are so distressing that he now actively scans his environment for anything that might trigger them. His office overlooks a wide, open plaza, a space that feels viscerally threatening to him. He has come to associate that feeling of exposure with the market square. As a result, he takes a ten-minute detour through cramped side streets each morning to avoid crossing it. He eats lunch at his desk, staring at spreadsheets, because the company cafeteria feels too vast and exposed. The most painful avoidance is reserved for a small, framed photo of himself and Evans, taken a week before the attack. He keeps it face down in his desk drawer, unable to bear the reminder of the friend he feels he lost, a grief he believes he has no right to. This isolation has not gone unnoticed; his team lead recently commented on his lack of engagement in group projects, a direct consequence of his silent withdrawal. Mateo came to therapy after his sister, during a tense family dinner, told him his eyes looked empty. He is here not with any real hope, but with a quiet fear that he is confirming what he already believes to be true: that he is broken beyond repair and has no future worth planning for.
